disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Vendor-neutral; no affiliation with any vendor. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original.

choices: Gradient descent — iteratively step opposite the gradient (scaled by learning rate) to minimize loss; too large diverges, too small crawls
Set weights randomly; gradients aren't needed
Gradient descent finds the global minimum always
Learning rate only affects speed, not convergence
scenarios.hint: If the loss landscape is a valley, which direction is downhill — and how big a step do you take?
scenarios.prompt: How does a model actually learn its parameters?
scenarios.situation: A neural net's loss isn't decreasing. The learning rate is 10.0. The team debates whether the model needs more layers.
scenarios.title: The diverging loss
scenarios.why: Gradient descent: compute the loss gradient w.r.t. parameters, step opposite to it by learning_rate × gradient. LR too large → overshoot/diverge (loss explodes or oscillates); too small → glacial convergence or stuck. It's the engine under linear regression, logistic regression, and neural nets. Before adding layers, check the optimizer basics: LR, and whether gradients vanish/explode.

choices: Bias-variance tradeoff — simple models underfit (high bias), complex models overfit (high variance); tune complexity (regularization, depth) to minimize total error on unseen data
More complexity always reduces total error
Bias and variance are unrelated
The tradeoff only applies to neural nets
scenarios.hint: A 1-parameter model vs a 1000-parameter model on 100 points — which errs from simplicity, which from memorization?
scenarios.prompt: What governs the choice of model complexity?
scenarios.situation: A deep tree gets 100% training accuracy but 60% on new data. A linear model gets 70% on both.
scenarios.title: The 100% training accuracy
scenarios.why: Total error = bias² + variance + noise. The deep tree: low bias, high variance — it memorized noise (overfitting). The linear model: higher bias, low variance — underfits but generalizes. The goal is the sweet spot minimizing validation error: control complexity via regularization (L1/L2), tree depth, early stopping. 100% training accuracy is a warning, not an achievement.

choices: Bayes' theorem — P(spam|words) ∝ P(words|spam)·P(spam); the base rate (prior) matters as much as the evidence
Count spammy words; priors don't matter
Naive Bayes assumes word order matters
Priors are always 50/50
scenarios.hint: If 1% of mail is spam, how strong must the word evidence be to call it spam?
scenarios.prompt: How does a Bayesian spam filter combine evidence with base rates?
scenarios.situation: A spam filter flags too much legitimate mail. Word evidence looks strong, but spam is only 1% of traffic.
scenarios.title: The Bayesian filter
scenarios.why: Bayes: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. Strong word evidence (likelihood) multiplied by a tiny prior (1% spam) can still yield a low spam probability — the base rate anchors the answer. Ignoring priors is the base-rate fallacy again. Naive Bayes adds the 'naive' independence assumption (words independent given class) — often wrong but empirically effective for text.

choices: Linear algebra: data as vectors/matrices; dot products measure similarity/projection; matrix multiplication composes transformations — it's the language models are written in
Matrices are just storage; the math doesn't matter
Dot products measure distance directly
Linear algebra is only for deep learning
scenarios.hint: What does w·x + b compute — and what is w, geometrically?
scenarios.prompt: Why is linear algebra the language of ML?
scenarios.situation: A junior asks why ML tutorials are full of matrices when 'it's just fitting lines'.
scenarios.title: The matrix question
scenarios.why: Every model is linear algebra: features are vectors, datasets are matrices, w·x+b is a projection (w defines the direction, b the offset), and layers compose via matrix multiplication. Similarity (cosine), projections (PCA), transformations (embeddings) — all linear algebra. You don't need proofs, but you need fluency: shapes, dot products, and what multiplication does geometrically.

choices: Distributions describe uncertainty: Gaussian for natural variation, Bernoulli/binomial for yes/no trials, and the CLT says sample means converge to Gaussian — the basis for confidence intervals
All data is Gaussian
Distributions are theoretical; real data ignores them
The CLT applies to single observations
scenarios.hint: Why can you put a confidence interval around a poll's 52% even though individual votes are yes/no?
scenarios.prompt: What do distributions buy you in practice?
scenarios.situation: A poll shows 52% ± 3%. The team asks where the ±3% comes from.
scenarios.title: The ±3%
scenarios.why: Bernoulli trials (each vote yes/no) → the sample proportion's sampling distribution is approximately Gaussian by the Central Limit Theorem → standard error = √(p(1-p)/n) → the ±3% margin. Distributions turn 'the data varies' into quantified uncertainty. Know the core three: Gaussian (measurement noise), Bernoulli/binomial (counts of yes/no), and when the CLT licenses normal approximations.

choices: Optimization (minimize loss) vs probability (model uncertainty) — most models are both: e.g., logistic regression minimizes cross-entropy = maximizes likelihood under a Bernoulli model
They are competing paradigms; pick one
Probability has no role in modern ML
Optimization is only for neural nets
scenarios.hint: What is cross-entropy loss actually maximizing?
scenarios.prompt: How do optimization and probability connect in ML?
scenarios.situation: A team debates 'loss minimization' vs 'probabilistic modeling' as competing approaches.
scenarios.title: The two views
scenarios.why: They're two views of one thing: minimizing cross-entropy = maximizing the likelihood of the data under the model (MLE); adding L2 regularization = MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior. The probabilistic view tells you what the loss means and how to quantify uncertainty; the optimization view tells you how to fit it. Logistic regression's loss isn't arbitrary — it's the negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli outcomes.

choices: Logistic regression — linear, calibrated probabilities, interpretable coefficients, fast; start simple and only add complexity when the baseline is beaten
Deep neural net — always best
k-NN — simplest to explain
Start with the most complex model available
scenarios.hint: If a simple model hits the target metric, what did the complex model buy you?
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined modeling workflow?
scenarios.situation: A team trains a 12-layer network for churn prediction. Nobody tried logistic regression. The network barely beats chance.
scenarios.title: The missing baseline
scenarios.why: Always start with a strong simple baseline (logistic/linear regression): it's interpretable, fast, calibrated, and sets the bar. Complexity must earn its place by beating the baseline on a proper validation split. Most business problems are solved (or well-served) by simple models; the fancy model needs to justify its opacity, latency, and maintenance. Baseline first, always.

choices: Trees split on feature thresholds to reduce impurity; forests average many trees trained on bootstrapped samples + random feature subsets — averaging kills the variance that makes single trees overfit
Forests grow one giant tree
Randomness hurts accuracy
Forests can't handle categoricals
scenarios.hint: One deep tree memorizes; 500 noisy trees vote — what happens to the memorization?
scenarios.prompt: Why do forests beat single trees?
scenarios.situation: A single decision tree overfits wildly. A random forest on the same data generalizes well.
scenarios.title: The forest advantage
scenarios.why: Single trees have high variance — small data changes reshape them. Forests bag: train each tree on a bootstrap sample with random feature subsets, then average/vote. Averaging uncorrelated errors cancels variance while keeping low bias. It's the bias-variance tradeoff in action: ensembling attacks variance. Cost: less interpretable than one tree (use feature importance/SHAP for insight).

choices: The margin — SVM finds the hyperplane maximizing the minimum distance to any training point; support vectors are the points on the margin boundary
SVM maximizes the number of support vectors
Kernels make data linearly separable by adding features manually
Margin size doesn't affect generalization
scenarios.hint: Which training points actually determine the boundary — all of them, or just the closest ones?
scenarios.prompt: What is the geometric intuition behind SVMs?
scenarios.situation: A team uses SVMs as a black box. Asked why it generalizes, they have no answer.
scenarios.title: The margin intuition
scenarios.why: SVM: the best separator isn't any line that splits the classes — it's the one with maximum margin (distance to the nearest points). Only the support vectors (points on/inside the margin) define the boundary; the rest are irrelevant. Kernels implicitly map to higher dimensions where separation is linear (RBF = infinite-dimensional). The margin intuition is why SVMs generalize: a fat margin tolerates new-point wobble.

choices: k-NN: lazy, no training — classify by the majority of the k nearest neighbors; choice of k trades noise (small k) vs oversmoothing (large k); distance metric and scaling dominate performance
k-NN builds a model during training
Large k always better
Scaling doesn't affect k-NN
scenarios.hint: With k=1, what does the decision boundary look like — smooth or jagged?
scenarios.prompt: How does k control the bias-variance tradeoff in k-NN?
scenarios.situation: k=1 gives 99% train / 65% test; k=50 gives 70%/68%.
scenarios.title: The k dial
scenarios.why: k-NN is lazy learning: no model, just stored points + a distance metric. k=1: jagged boundaries, memorizes noise (high variance). Large k: smooth boundaries, may wash out local structure (high bias). And the hidden dial: feature scaling — without it, the largest-scale feature dominates all distances. k-NN teaches that 'simple' methods still have crucial hyperparameters.

choices: Regression predicts continuous values (price), classification predicts categories (churn yes/no) — the loss, metrics, and output layer all follow from this; some problems convert (predict probability, threshold it)
They are the same; only the algorithm differs
Regression can't output probabilities
Classification is always easier
scenarios.hint: 'How much will they spend?' vs 'will they churn?' — which output type each?
scenarios.prompt: How do you frame the problem type?
scenarios.situation: A team applies classification metrics (accuracy) to a price-prediction model.
scenarios.title: The framing error
scenarios.why: Regression: continuous target (MSE/MAE metrics). Classification: discrete classes (accuracy/precision/recall/AUC). The framing dictates loss functions, metrics, and interpretation — accuracy on a regression problem is meaningless. Bridge: predict churn probability (regression on [0,1]) then threshold for decisions (classification). Frame first: what decision will this output drive?

choices: Neural net basics: layers of learned features, trained by backprop (gradient descent via chain rule); depth buys representational power at the cost of data/compute/tuning
More layers always help
Backprop is unrelated to gradient descent
Neural nets don't overfit
scenarios.hint: What does each layer compute from the previous layer's output?
scenarios.prompt: What is the core idea of a neural network?
scenarios.situation: A team treats neural nets as magic. Asked what depth adds, they say 'accuracy'.
scenarios.title: The layer intuition
scenarios.why: A net composes learned transformations: each layer builds features from the previous layer's (edges → shapes → objects in vision). Training = backpropagation applying the chain rule to push gradients through every layer, then gradient descent. Depth enables hierarchical features but demands data, compute, and tuning (LR, init, regularization). 'More layers = more accuracy' fails without those — depth is capacity, and capacity needs control.

choices: k-means: assign points to nearest centroid, recompute centroids, repeat — sensitive to k, initialization, scaling, and cluster shape (spherical); choose k via elbow/silhouette + domain sense
k-means finds the true k automatically
It handles non-spherical clusters well
Initialization doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: Run it twice with different seeds — do you get the same clusters?
scenarios.prompt: How does k-means work, and what are its fragilities?
scenarios.situation: Customer segmentation with k-means gives different segments on every run; elongated clusters are split.
scenarios.title: The unstable segments
scenarios.why: k-means alternates: assign-to-nearest-centroid, move-centroids-to-means, until convergence — to a local optimum, hence seed sensitivity (use k-means++ init + multiple restarts). It assumes spherical, similar-sized clusters; elongated or varied-density shapes get mangled. Choose k with elbow/silhouette scores plus business sense ('do 7 segments mean anything?'). Scale features first — k-means is distance-based.

choices: PCA — project onto the directions of maximum variance; keep enough components to explain ~90-95% variance; it's linear, so nonlinear structure needs other methods
PCA selects the most important original features
Components are interpretable as features
PCA is nonlinear
scenarios.hint: If 50 sensors are highly correlated, how many underlying signals are there really?
scenarios.prompt: When and how do you use PCA?
scenarios.situation: 50 correlated sensor features; models overfit and train slowly. The team wants fewer features without losing signal.
scenarios.title: The 50 sensors
scenarios.why: PCA finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance; the top components capture most signal in fewer dimensions (check cumulative explained variance — keep ~90-95%). Use for: visualization (2-3 components), denoising, speeding up models. Caveats: components are linear combos (not interpretable features), it needs scaling, and it only captures linear structure (nonlinear → consider UMAP/t-SNE for viz, autoencoders for modeling).

choices: Anomaly detection: isolation forest / one-class SVM / autoencoder reconstruction error — model 'normal', flag deviations; tune the contamination/threshold to the operational cost of false alarms
Train a classifier on anomalies — you have plenty of labels
Anomalies can't be detected unsupervised
Threshold choice doesn't matter
scenarios.hint: With 10 frauds in 1M transactions, what do you train on?
scenarios.prompt: How do you catch rare events with (almost) no labels?
scenarios.situation: Fraud: 10 known cases in 1M transactions. The team wants a classifier.
scenarios.title: The rare fraud
scenarios.why: Supervised learning starves on 10 positives. Instead: model normality (isolation forest isolates anomalies with few splits; autoencoders reconstruct normal well, anomalies poorly) and flag deviations. The threshold is a business decision: each false alarm costs investigator time, each miss costs fraud loss — tune to that tradeoff. Evaluate with the few labels via precision@k, not accuracy.

choices: Hierarchical clustering — builds a dendrogram (agglomerative: merge closest); cut at the height that gives meaningful groups; no k needed upfront
Hierarchies require k upfront
Dendrograms are just visualizations
It's faster than k-means at scale
scenarios.hint: What does the tree show that a flat k-means assignment doesn't?
scenarios.prompt: When is hierarchical clustering the right choice?
scenarios.situation: A biologist wants to see relationships among gene-expression profiles at multiple granularities, not one flat partition.
scenarios.title: The dendrogram
scenarios.why: Agglomerative clustering merges closest clusters bottom-up, producing a dendrogram — structure at every granularity. Cut the tree where the branches are meaningful (long vertical gaps = natural splits). No k upfront; the hierarchy itself is the insight. Cost: O(n²)-ish scaling — fine for thousands, not millions. Choose linkage (ward, complete, average) deliberately; it shapes the tree.

choices: Clustering is for discovery, not prediction — validate with stability, interpretability, and downstream usefulness; 'clusters' may be artifacts of the algorithm
Clusters are real by definition
Validation isn't possible unsupervised
More clusters always better
scenarios.hint: k-means will return 5 clusters from pure noise — how do you know yours aren't noise?
scenarios.prompt: How do you know the clusters mean anything?
scenarios.situation: k-means returns 5 customer segments. Marketing asks: 'Are these real?'
scenarios.title: The five segments
scenarios.why: Clustering always returns clusters — even from noise. Validate: stability across seeds/samples, silhouette/cohesion scores, and crucially, interpretability ('can we name them?') and actionability (do they behave differently on metrics we care about?). A segment that doesn't differ on any business metric is numerology. Unsupervised results need supervised-style skepticism.

choices: Topic modeling / embeddings for text: LDA discovers themes; embeddings + clustering groups by meaning — validate topics by reading documents, not just coherence scores
Word counts are enough for themes
Topics are objective truth
Embeddings can't be clustered
scenarios.hint: How do you check a topic is real — the score, or reading its top documents?
scenarios.prompt: How do you discover themes in documents?
scenarios.situation: 10k support tickets; the team wants to know 'what are people complaining about?'
scenarios.title: The ticket themes
scenarios.why: LDA models each document as a mixture of topics (word distributions); modern alternative: embed documents, cluster the embeddings. Either way, validate by reading top documents per topic — coherence scores help, but human judgment decides if 'Topic 7' is a real theme or word salad. Name topics from evidence, then quantify: topic share over time shows emerging issues.

choices: 99% accuracy on 99%-negative data = the majority-class baseline (predict 'no' always); use precision/recall, PR-AUC, or balanced metrics — accuracy lies on imbalanced data
99% accuracy is excellent regardless
The model is 99% good
Imbalanced data doesn't affect accuracy
evidence: Predicted: 990 TN, 0 TP, 10 FN → accuracy = 990/1000 = 99%, recall = 0%
scenarios.hint: What does a model that always predicts 'not fraud' score?
scenarios.prompt: Why is 99% accuracy worthless here?
scenarios.situation: Fraud model: 99% accuracy, but it catches zero frauds.
scenarios.title: The 99% model
scenarios.why: On 99%-negative data, 'always predict negative' scores 99% accuracy with zero recall — the accuracy paradox. Report the confusion matrix: precision (of flagged, how many true), recall (of true, how many caught), and PR-AUC (better than ROC-AUC for heavy imbalance). Choose the metric from the cost: missed fraud (recall) vs false alarms (precision). Accuracy is the wrong metric whenever classes are imbalanced or costs are asymmetric.

choices: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) (exactness: of alarms, how many real); Recall = TP/(TP+FN) (completeness: of real cases, how many caught) — threshold trades one for the other; F1 balances them
Precision and recall are the same
Threshold doesn't affect them
F1 is always the right single metric
scenarios.hint: Spam filter: is it worse to miss a spam or to trash a real email?
scenarios.prompt: How do precision and recall trade off?
scenarios.situation: A spam filter catches 99% of spam but trashes 5% of real mail. Users revolt.
scenarios.title: The aggressive filter
scenarios.why: Precision (don't cry wolf) vs recall (don't miss the wolf): lowering the threshold catches more spam (recall ↑) but trashes more real mail (precision ↓). The operating point is a business decision: for spam, precision matters (losing real mail is costly); for cancer screening, recall matters (missing a case is costly). Tune the threshold to the cost asymmetry; F1 is a neutral compromise, not a universal answer.

choices: Train/validation/test: train fits, validation selects (hyperparameters, models), test estimates final performance — used once; touching test during selection leaks optimism into the estimate
Test set can guide tuning — it's just data
Validation and test are interchangeable
One split is enough for everything
scenarios.hint: If you pick the best of 50 models on the test set, what have you fit to the test set?
scenarios.prompt: Why three splits, and what breaks if you tune on test?
scenarios.situation: A team tunes hyperparameters against the test set, then reports test accuracy as 'expected performance'.
scenarios.title: The touched test set
scenarios.why: Validation = the selection instrument (try 50 configs, pick the best). Test = the measuring instrument (one honest estimate of unseen performance). Tuning on test = fitting to it — the estimate becomes optimistic (you selected for test luck). Keep test locked until final evaluation. For small data: cross-validation on train, held-out test at the end. Leakage anywhere inflates every number you report.

choices: k-fold cross-validation — rotate which fold validates, average the scores; stratified for classification; essential on small data; still keep a held-out test for the final estimate
Single split is always sufficient
CV replaces the test set
More folds always better regardless of cost
scenarios.hint: With 500 samples, how much can you trust one lucky/unlucky split?
scenarios.prompt: When and how do you use cross-validation?
scenarios.situation: 500 samples; a single 80/20 split gives wildly different scores across random seeds.
scenarios.title: The unstable split
scenarios.why: k-fold CV: split into k folds, train on k-1, validate on the held-out fold, rotate — every point validates once. Average ± std gives a stable estimate with uncertainty. Stratified k-fold preserves class ratios (critical for imbalance). Use CV for model/hyperparameter selection on small data; still hold out a final test set. Cost: k trainings — 5-10 folds is the usual tradeoff.

choices: ROC-AUC: ranking quality across thresholds (probability a random positive outranks a random negative); PR-AUC better for imbalance; neither replaces choosing an operating threshold
AUC 0.9 means 90% accuracy
ROC is best for imbalanced data
AUC picks your threshold
scenarios.hint: Two models, same AUC — can they need different thresholds in production?
scenarios.prompt: What does AUC actually measure?
scenarios.situation: Two models both have AUC 0.9. The team declares them equivalent.
scenarios.title: The equal AUCs
scenarios.why: ROC-AUC measures ranking: given a random positive and negative, P(positive scores higher) — threshold-independent. Same AUC ≠ same operating behavior: the curves can cross, meaning model A is better at high-precision operating points and B at high-recall ones. For imbalanced data, PR-AUC is more informative (ROC looks rosy when negatives dominate). AUC compares rankers; the threshold decision still needs precision/recall at the operating point.

choices: Leakage: features containing future/target info (e.g., 'cancellation_reason' predicting churn) — audit features for 'would I know this at prediction time?'; time-based splits expose it
Leakage only happens with duplicate rows
High validation scores prove no leakage
Leakage is rare
scenarios.hint: If the feature wouldn't exist yet when the prediction is made, what is it?
scenarios.prompt: How do you detect target leakage?
scenarios.situation: Churn model: 98% validation accuracy. Top feature: 'days_since_cancellation'. Production performance: coin flip.
scenarios.title: The too-good model
scenarios.why: 'Days since cancellation' is known only after churn — target leakage. The model learned the answer key. Detection: ask 'could I compute this feature at prediction time?' for every feature; use time-based splits (train on past, validate on future) which break leakage's illusion; beware IDs, post-event timestamps, and aggregates over the target window. Suspiciously perfect validation is the smell — investigate, don't celebrate.

choices: One-hot for low-cardinality nominals; target/mean encoding (with CV/regularization) or embeddings for high-cardinality; ordinal encoding only for true ordinals — never label-encode nominals for linear models
Label-encode everything — numbers are numbers
One-hot 10k zip codes — sparsity is fine
Encoding choice doesn't matter for trees
scenarios.hint: What does label-encoding 'red=1, blue=2, green=3' tell a linear model about colors?
scenarios.prompt: How do you encode categoricals?
scenarios.situation: A 'city' feature with 2,000 values; a 'color' feature label-encoded 1-5 for a linear model.
scenarios.title: The encoding choices
scenarios.why: Label encoding imposes a false order (green > blue?) that linear models take literally — use one-hot for nominals (each category its own binary). High cardinality (2,000 cities): one-hot explodes — use target encoding (mean target per category, computed with cross-validation to avoid leakage) or learned embeddings. Trees tolerate label encoding (splits don't assume order linearity) but still prefer one-hot for low-cardinality. Match encoding to cardinality and model.

choices: Scale for distance/gradient methods (k-NN, SVM, neural nets, regularized regression) — standardize (zero mean/unit variance) or min-max; trees don't need it
Scaling is always required
Trees need scaled features
Standardize categoricals too
scenarios.hint: In k-NN, if income is in dollars and age in years, which dominates the distance?
scenarios.prompt: When does scaling matter?
scenarios.situation: k-NN performs terribly; income (tens of thousands) swamps age (tens) in distances.
scenarios.title: The swamped distance
scenarios.why: Distance-based (k-NN, SVM, clustering) and gradient-based (neural nets, regularized linear models) methods are scale-sensitive: large-magnitude features dominate. Standardize (z-score) or normalize (min-max) numeric features — fit the scaler on train, apply to validation/test (fitting on all = leakage). Tree models split per-feature, so they're scale-invariant. Rule: scale when geometry or gradients care; skip when trees decide.

choices: Missingness is information: add missing-indicator features, then impute (median/mode, or model-based) — and ask why it's missing (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) because the mechanism matters
Always drop rows with missing values
Mean-impute everything blindly
Missing values can be ignored by all models
scenarios.hint: If 'income missing' correlates with churn, what does dropping those rows destroy?
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle missing values thoughtfully?
scenarios.situation: 30% of incomes missing. Dropping rows loses a third of data; the missingness correlates with the target.
scenarios.title: The missing incomes
scenarios.why: First ask why: MCAR (random), MAR (explained by other features), MNAR (missingness itself informative — e.g., high earners skip the question). Then: add is_missing indicators (the pattern often predicts), impute sensibly (median/mode; never mean on skewed data without thought), or use models handling missingness natively. Dropping MNAR rows biases everything downstream — the missingness was signal.

choices: Temporal leakage in features: any aggregate including the target window or future data (e.g., 'total spend' including post-churn months) — compute features strictly from data available at prediction time
Aggregates are always safe
Leakage only affects labels
Future data in features is fine if the model is regularized
scenarios.hint: 'Average monthly spend' computed over the customer's whole lifetime — including after they churned. What's wrong?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most dangerous feature-engineering mistake?
scenarios.situation: A churn model uses 'lifetime average spend' — computed over the full history including post-churn months. Validation is stellar; production fails.
scenarios.title: The future in the features
scenarios.why: Point-in-time correctness: every feature must be computable from data available at prediction time. Lifetime aggregates leak the future (post-churn months have zero spend — the model 'learns' churn from its own consequence). Build features with as-of joins (data as known at prediction time). This is the #1 silent killer of ML projects: great offline, garbage live.

choices: Domain-driven interaction/polynomial features, binning, and datetime decomposition (hour/day-of-week/month) — create what the model can't easily learn; validate with ablation
More features always help
Feature engineering is obsolete with deep learning
Datetime as a single timestamp is fine
scenarios.hint: Can a linear model learn 'weekend vs weekday' from a raw timestamp?
scenarios.prompt: What features do you create, and why?
scenarios.situation: A demand model uses raw timestamps. It misses weekly seasonality a linear model can't see.
scenarios.title: The hidden seasonality
scenarios.why: Models can't learn what they can't represent: decompose datetimes (hour, weekday, month, holiday flags), create ratios/interactions the domain suggests (debt-to-income, not just debt and income), bin nonlinear relationships. Then ablate: does the feature actually help validation? Feature engineering is hypothesis-driven — encode domain knowledge as model-readable signals, and prune what doesn't earn its keep (curse of dimensionality is real).

choices: Select by validation impact (ablation, permutation importance), not univariate correlation — drop what doesn't help the model; beware selection bias from selecting on the same data you evaluate on
Keep all features; models ignore useless ones
Univariate correlation is sufficient for selection
Feature selection is only for interpretability
scenarios.hint: A feature with zero univariate correlation can be crucial in combination — what does filtering by correlation miss?
scenarios.prompt: How do you prune the feature set?
scenarios.situation: 200 features; the model overfits. Univariate filtering drops features that matter in combination.
scenarios.title: The 200 features
scenarios.why: Select by model-measured impact: permutation importance, SHAP values, or ablation (remove and re-validate) — these capture interactions that univariate screens miss. Regularization (L1) selects during training. Caveat: selecting features on the validation set then reporting on it is optimistic — nest selection inside CV. Fewer, better features: faster training, less overfitting, easier debugging.

choices: Training/serving skew — features computed differently (batch vs realtime), stale encodings, or time drift; enforce point-in-time feature pipelines shared by train and serve
The model is just bad; retrain blindly
Skew is unavoidable; accept it
Serving code can differ from training code
scenarios.hint: 'Average spend last 30 days' — computed how, in training vs in the live API?
scenarios.prompt: What causes the offline/online gap?
scenarios.situation: Validation AUC 0.85, production 0.62. Features are 'the same' — but training used batch-computed aggregates, serving uses a streaming approximation.
scenarios.title: The offline-online gap
scenarios.why: Training/serving skew: the model sees different feature distributions live than in training — different computation (batch vs streaming), different missing-value handling, stale lookup tables, or simple time drift. Fix: one feature pipeline serving both (feature store), with logged production features to compare distributions against training. Debug by scoring logged live features offline — if offline-on-live-features is also bad, it's skew, not the model.

choices: Monitor: input distribution drift (PSI/KS tests), prediction distribution shifts, and business metrics (conversion, default rate) — alert on drift before performance visibly decays
Monitor accuracy — labels arrive instantly
Drift doesn't affect models
Retrain on a fixed schedule blindly
scenarios.hint: Labels arrive weeks late — what can you monitor today?
scenarios.prompt: How do you know a model degraded when labels lag?
scenarios.situation: Loan defaults take months to materialize. The model's live quality is unknowable in real time.
scenarios.title: The silent decay
scenarios.why: When labels lag, monitor proxies: input feature drift (population shift changing P(X)), prediction distribution shifts (the model suddenly scores everyone high-risk), and leading business indicators. Statistical tests (PSI, KS) quantify drift per feature. Set retraining triggers on drift thresholds + scheduled refreshes, not on accuracy you can't measure yet. A model without monitoring is a rumor.

choices: Shadow/champion-challenger or A/B test the model — route a fraction of traffic, compare business metrics (not just ML metrics), with a rollback plan
Ship to 100% immediately; validation was good
ML metrics guarantee business impact
A/B testing models is impossible
scenarios.hint: The model improves AUC — does it improve revenue? How would you know?
scenarios.prompt: How do you deploy a model safely?
scenarios.situation: A new recommender beats the old on offline NDCG. The team wants to ship to everyone.
scenarios.title: The model rollout
scenarios.why: Offline metrics ≠ business impact. Deploy like software: shadow mode (score live, don't act — validate the pipeline), then champion/challenger (fraction of traffic, randomized), measuring business metrics (revenue, conversion) with a kill switch. Models interact with the world they predict (feedback loops) — only live measurement captures that. Rollback plan first, celebration later.

choices: Version everything: code, data snapshot, hyperparameters, and the model artifact (MLflow/registry) — reproducibility requires the full lineage, not just the pickle file
Version the model file only
Git on notebooks is enough
Data doesn't need versioning
scenarios.hint: 'Which data trained model v3?' — can you answer?
scenarios.prompt: What does model versioning actually cover?
scenarios.situation: A production bug traces to 'model v3', but nobody knows which data, code, or params produced it.
scenarios.title: The mystery model
scenarios.why: A model artifact without lineage is unreproducible: version the training code (git), the data snapshot (or query + timestamp), hyperparameters, environment, and metrics — linked in a registry (MLflow, etc.). Then 'v3' resolves to a complete, rebuildable recipe. Debugging, auditing, and rollback all depend on this. The pickle file is the least important part of the version.

choices: Feedback loops — the model's actions change the world it learns from (e.g., rejecting applicants removes their outcomes); detect via exploration/holdouts, correct with careful causal design
Feedback loops don't occur in ML
More data fixes feedback loops
Retraining solves it automatically
scenarios.hint: If the model rejects an applicant, do you ever learn whether they'd have repaid?
scenarios.prompt: What breaks when the model shapes its own training data?
scenarios.situation: A lending model trained on approved loans only; rejections never generate outcomes. Performance decays as policy shifts the applicant pool.
scenarios.title: The self-fulfilling model
scenarios.why: Selective labels: you only observe outcomes for the model's past decisions (approved loans) — the training data is censored by the model itself. Retraining on this data amplifies the bias (reject more → learn less about the rejected). Mitigations: exploration (approve a random holdout), reject inference techniques, and causal framing. Recognize when your data is a consequence of your model — that's the loop.

choices: Latency/throughput/cost engineering: batch vs realtime serving, model compression (quantization, distillation), caching, and autoscaling — the best model you can't serve is the wrong model
Accuracy is the only deployment criterion
Serving infrastructure doesn't affect model choice
Latency is fixed regardless of model
scenarios.hint: The model scores in 800ms; the SLA is 100ms. What are your levers?
scenarios.prompt: How do you meet a serving SLA?
scenarios.situation: Best-accuracy model: 800ms p99 latency. Product SLA: 100ms.
scenarios.title: The latency wall
scenarios.why: Serving is engineering: batch inference for non-urgent scoring, realtime APIs for interactive; compression levers — quantization (smaller/faster, slight accuracy cost), distillation (small model mimics large), pruning; caching frequent inputs; autoscaling replicas. Sometimes the answer is a simpler model meeting the SLA at 95% of the accuracy. The deployable model beats the accurate-but-unservable one — co-design model and serving.
